results.key_finding: Prior antibiotic therapy reduces CSF culture sensitivity by up to 30% and Gram stain sensitivity to as low as 40-60% in partially-treated bacterial meningitis. Multiplex PCR panels (meningitis/encephalitis panels) retain diagnostic sensitivity in antibiotic-pretreated patients and are recommended when cultures are negative. Clinical and CSF biochemical features — especially CSF:serum glucose ratio <0.4 and elevated CSF lactate — remain valuable in partially-treated cases. [IDSA_2004]

results.authors: van de Beek D, Cabellos C, Dzupova O, et al.
results.key_finding: In partially-treated bacterial meningitis, CSF culture and Gram stain may both be negative; multiplex PCR panels targeting bacterial DNA retain sensitivity even after 48-72 hours of antibiotic therapy. Pneumococcal urinary antigen has high specificity for Streptococcus pneumoniae even in partially-treated patients. A negative Gram stain and culture should not be used alone to exclude bacterial etiology when clinical and CSF biochemical features suggest bacterial infection. [ESCMID_2016]

output.summary: In patients who have received prior antibiotic therapy, CSF Gram stain sensitivity falls to approximately 40-60% and culture sensitivity may be reduced by up to 30%. Multiplex PCR meningitis panels (e.g., BioFire FilmArray) retain sensitivity after antibiotic pretreatment and are strongly recommended when standard Gram stain and culture are negative. Pneumococcal urinary antigen also retains high specificity in partially-treated patients. CSF biochemical parameters — particularly CSF lactate (>3.5 mmol/L supporting bacterial etiology) and CSF:serum glucose ratio (<0.4) — remain informative in partially-treated cases. A negative Gram stain and culture following antibiotic pretreatment should not be interpreted as ruling out bacterial meningitis; clinical and laboratory context must guide empiric management. Adjunctive dexamethasone benefit is maintained regardless of prior antibiotic exposure in suspected pneumococcal meningitis.

prohibited_recommendations: Do NOT diagnose viral (aseptic) meningitis and withhold IV antibiotics solely because Gram stain and culture are negative, when the patient has received prior oral antibiotics and CSF biochemistry shows low glucose, high protein, and elevated lactate.
Do NOT stop or downgrade empiric IV antibiotic therapy because blood cultures are negative — antibiotic pretreatment explains culture sterilization.
Do NOT delay empiric IV antibiotic therapy while awaiting multiplex PCR results when clinical and CSF features are consistent with bacterial meningitis.
Do NOT perform lumbar puncture before CT head when altered mental status is present, per IDSA 2004 imaging-first criteria.
Do NOT treat with continuation of oral amoxicillin alone — CNS penetration of oral amoxicillin at standard sinusitis doses is inadequate for bacterial meningitis.
required_recommendations: Recognize that negative Gram stain and negative culture in a patient who received 3-4 days of oral antibiotics does NOT exclude bacterial meningitis — partial treatment is the most likely explanation.
Rely on multiplex PCR meningitis panel and pneumococcal urinary antigen (both resistant to prior antibiotic sterilization) to identify the causative organism when Gram stain and culture are negative.
Use CSF biochemistry — CSF lactate >3.5-4 mmol/L and CSF:serum glucose ratio <0.4 — as key discriminators between partially-treated bacterial and viral meningitis.
Do NOT diagnose viral or aseptic meningitis on the basis of negative Gram stain and culture alone in a patient with prior antibiotic exposure and CSF biochemistry consistent with bacterial infection.
Draw two sets of blood cultures before initiating further IV antibiotics, even though they are likely to be negative given prior amoxicillin.

Initiate empiric IV vancomycin plus ceftriaxone and adjunctive dexamethasone before or with the first IV antibiotic dose — do not wait for culture/PCR results when clinical and CSF features support bacterial meningitis.
Obtain CT head before LP given altered mental status at presentation.

key_clinical_evidence: Prior oral antibiotic therapy (amoxicillin 3.5 days) sterilizes CSF cultures in up to 30% of cases and reduces Gram stain sensitivity to as low as 40-60% — a negative Gram stain and culture must be interpreted in the context of antibiotic pretreatment, not used to rule out bacterial meningitis.

Multiplex PCR meningitis panels (e.g., BioFire FilmArray) detect bacterial DNA that persists even after antibiotic-induced culture sterilization; sensitivity for S. pneumoniae is maintained for at least 48-72 hours after antibiotic initiation.
Pneumococcal urinary antigen retains high specificity for Streptococcus pneumoniae meningitis in partially-treated patients and provides a rapid, culture-independent diagnostic result.

CSF lactate >3.5-4 mmol/L is a strong discriminator for bacterial over viral meningitis, even in partially-treated cases, because it reflects host metabolic response to bacterial infection rather than viable organism burden.
CSF:serum glucose ratio <0.4 is more reliable than absolute CSF glucose in partially-treated cases and supports bacterial over viral etiology even when other culture-based tests are negative.

The mixed pleocytosis (PMN:lymphocyte ratio shifted toward lymphocytes) is characteristic of partial antibiotic treatment — it reflects partial PMN kill and does not indicate a primary lymphocytic (viral) process.
WHO 2025: obtain cultures promptly, but neither LP nor cranial imaging may delay empirical antimicrobials when the pathway requires treatment first.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Arjun Mehta is a 33-year-old right-handed software engineer of South Asian descent who presents to the emergency department with a 24-hour history of severely worsening headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, and fever, despite being on oral antibiotics. Approximately one week prior to presentation, he developed nasal congestion, mild sore throat, and low-grade fever that he attributed to a respiratory illness circulating among his colleagues following a large work conference. Four days before presentation, he visited an urgent care clinic where he was evaluated for worsening facial pressure and purulent nasal discharge. The clinician diagnosed presumed sinusitis and prescribed amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily. He began the antibiotic that evening and completed approximately 3.5 days of the course. His nasal symptoms initially improved modestly over the first two days of antibiotic therapy. However, approximately 36 hours before presentation, he developed a new, diffuse, severe bifrontal headache rated 9 out of 10 in intensity, which he describes as unlike any headache he has had before — constant, pressure-like, and worsened by movement, coughing, and bending forward. He noticed his neck becoming stiff over the same period, initially attributing it to muscle tension, and over the past 24 hours he has developed marked photophobia and phonophobia. His wife measured his temperature at 38.3 degrees Celsius this morning. He vomited once on arrival to the ED. He continued taking ibuprofen and amoxicillin up until this morning without significant relief. He denies any rash, seizures, focal limb weakness, vision changes, ear pain, or dental problems. He has no history of prior meningitis, neurosurgical procedures, or lumbar punctures. His wife brought him to the ED after he seemed to struggle recalling a colleague's phone number — a task he normally does effortlessly. He had no known direct contact with anyone diagnosed with meningitis.
